after.name: Question 1
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t/3}-1.$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=e+1.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=3?$
after.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =(e+1)+{\int }_{0}^{3}({e}^{t/3}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =e+1+{[3{e}^{t/3}-t]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =e+1+([3{e}^{(3)/3}-(3)]-[3{e}^{(0)/3}-(0)]) \\  & =e+1+([3e-3]-[3]) \\  & =e+1+3e-6 \\  & =4e-5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=4e-5.$

after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t-1}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=2.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
after.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =2+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{[{e}^{t-1}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+({e}^{2-1}-{e}^{1-1}) \\  & =2+({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2+e-1 \\  & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=e+1.$

content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t-1}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=2.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
content.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =2+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{[{e}^{t-1}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+({e}^{2-1}-{e}^{1-1}) \\  & =2+({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2+e-1 \\  & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=e+1.$
